# Applications for Eric Rash: Deep Reinforcement Learning for NBA Player Valuation

## Where this applies

1. Inference: Context-weighting football performance data by game state. The speaker's point is that an identical action is worth far more when the game is close [03:04]. For football, garbage-time snaps could inflate or deflate PFF grades and GPS game loads. Tag snaps as close or blowout and see whether a player's grade or load changes when blowout snaps are set aside.
2. Inference: Offensive line unit fit. The talk argues that player values are not additive and that pairs can be synergistic or anti-synergistic [10:10]. Offensive line grades from PFF are per player; look at whether five-man combinations that played together show results that a simple sum of grades misses.
3. Inference: Deciding how long to wait before trusting a new player's number. The speaker says his method stabilizes in about 3 weeks versus 2 months for RAPM [07:08]. The Baylor version of this is a written rule for how many games or test weeks a transfer or early-enrolled player needs before his grade moves a recruiting or playing-time decision.
4. Inference: Reading defensive value that box scores miss. The speaker argues defensive specialists are undervalued by traditional metrics [09:40]. When PFF defensive grades and counting stats disagree for a player, treat the disagreement as a question for film, not a tie-break.

## Eric's baseline

No direct link found. The talk is about NBA valuation models and front-office roster construction; Eric's baseline covers testing, monitoring, force plates, GPS and programming, and does not state a position on player-valuation models or synergy.

## What would have to be true

- A win probability or expected points model for football that Baylor trusts, and play-by-play data with game state. The talk used about five seasons of NBA play-by-play [16:21]; the football equivalent has not been shown here.
- For lineup or unit synergy: enough snaps with the same five or the same pair together. A questioner in the Q&A raised exactly this problem (players who nearly always play together) [16:21].
- For any stabilization rule: a way to test it on Baylor's own past seasons.

## Do not apply when

- The decision rests on the talk's headline numbers (the 5 plus win fit effect [11:11], 89 synergies and 61 anti-synergies [10:10]). They come from NBA data with no shown uncertainty, and a judge questioned the portability of Shapley values across lineups [13:13].
- The roster is college football. Rosters turn over yearly, units are larger (11 on each side), and NBA lineup results do not transfer to offensive line continuity without checking.
- Sample sizes are small. The speaker himself says new players require extrapolation and that accuracy is limited there [16:21].
- Do not read the predictive results as beating the market: the Vegas line benchmark was still best [11:42].

## First step

Pick one Baylor game and mark each snap close or blowout using a simple score margin and quarter rule. Compare two or three players' PFF grades with and without the blowout snaps. One spreadsheet, nothing changes in practice.

# Applications for Eric Rash: From Noise to Knowledge, Research for Female Athletes

## Where this applies

1. Inference: A validation check before adopting any wearable or sleep and cycle-tracking product with Baylor women's teams. The speaker's workflow asks whether the device has been validated against a trusted standard, whether it reproduces known values, and whether the sample is diverse [33:19][33:51]. Write that as a one-page checklist and apply it to each consumer device a sport coach or athlete proposes.
2. Inference: Recording how menstrual status is determined (asked, hormone-tested, on a birth control pill with withdrawal bleed) in any internal monitoring for women's teams. The speaker says asking is not the same as testing, and that a withdrawal bleed is not a natural cycle [16:25]. Any internal analysis that groups athletes by cycle phase needs that field first.
3. Inference: Applying her audit fields to the Zotero library for any women's-sport question: population, athlete caliber tier, menstrual status method, research theme, journal, sample size [15:23][16:56]. This lets Eric see quickly whether a study's athletes resemble collegiate athletes (her tier scale runs 0 to 5, with tier 2 at three workouts a week with intent to compete [15:54]).
4. Inference: Routing under-fueling and low energy availability questions to Athletic Medicine and Performance Nutrition, with Applied Performance supplying monitoring data. The speaker names relative energy deficiency in sport as very prevalent and partly inadvertent under-fueling [07:10].
5. Inference: Survey design for any staff survey of women athletes, using her listed weaknesses (cross-sectional, selection, recall and non-response bias) as the critique list [27:41][28:12].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys rolled out from summer 2022 were dropped after about a year because athletes learned to game them; they are kept for return-to-play and chronic conditions. The talk extends this: it lists different survey weaknesses (bias types) and still treats surveys as useful for prevalence and early ideas [27:41]. It does not mention athletes gaming answers.
- Eric's baseline: modified reactive strength index from daily CMJ was chosen over surveys because it is objective, consistent and actionable. The talk agrees with preferring validated measures, and adds that validity has to be shown against a gold standard [29:14].
- Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data." The talk agrees: poor data in with poor analysis gives a poor conclusion [34:22].

---
type: video-summary
video_id: AZlacK4gE4k
title: "SSAC26: The History of Progress in Football Analytics"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Eric Eager]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Eric Eager, introduced as Vice President of Football Analytics at the Carolina Panthers, traces football analytics from the 1970 expected points paper through decades of little progress to fast change over roughly the last five years. He credits public play-by-play data, companies that sold contextual data, and tracking data. He expects AI and transformer models to accelerate this further. He argues that data engineering remains the limiting step, and that analysts must communicate in uncertainty, meet football staff most of the way, and admit what they do not know, or the work will not be adopted.

## Key claims

- Expected points started with a 1970 paper by Virgil Carter, and football analytics then made little progress until the late 1980s. [02:34]
- The 1989 Herschel Walker trade is an analytical story because of the draft value chart that let Dallas turn the acquired picks into more and better ones, while the Rams, who had no such tool, used the Colts picks as they came. [04:07]
- Nearly 40 years passed with almost no progress beyond the expected points idea. [05:08]
- Public play-by-play data (nflscrapR in 2017, nflfastR in 2020) let many people estimate win probability, expected points added, expected YAC and completion probability over expected, and many of those people now work in the NFL. [05:08] [05:38]
- Fourth-down aggressiveness rose sharply: in 2021 more than half of teams were going for it when the model said to, and fourth-down attempts per team per game are about three times the 1980s rate. [06:09] [06:40]
- Public work shaped internal team work: dropback type, play action, coverage, pressure and coverage shell were discussed outside the game and then inside it. [07:41]
- Motion rates have risen sharply, and 2021 was the first time a team (the Rams, who won the Super Bowl) disguised coverage on more than half of snaps. [08:12]
- Early player-value work showed interior defensive linemen as less valuable than edge players; with more two-high safeties and lighter boxes, the interior defensive line market has risen. [09:45] [10:16]
- Tracking data (X and Y position, direction and orientation every tenth of a second) lets analysts ask harder questions, such as sharper fourth-down calls now that the ball is chipped, and the play-action trade-off for linebackers. [11:16] [11:47] [12:17]
- Tracking-based credit attribution (transformer models) now reveals hidden contributions, with tackling and positioning as the example, and the speaker questions whether tackle counts measure the right thing. [14:19] [14:49] [15:19]
- Tooling and AI are producing insights faster than people can look at them, so there is a need to pause and review before generating more. [16:20]
- Communication matters as much as the math; if the field moves at a pace no one understands, no one adopts. [17:51]
- Building tools for football people works best by meeting them 95% of the way and nudging, and building momentum with people can be worth more than the highest expected value idea. Saying "I don't know" protects credibility. [18:23] [18:53] [19:24]
- There will be push-back toward traditional risk-taking, such as after a failed fourth down in the AFC Championship game; his view is that he has never regretted knowing more. [16:51] [17:21]

## Numbers and definitions

- 1970: year of the Carter expected points paper. [02:34]
- 1 and 15: the Cowboys' 1989 record. [03:04]
- 2017 and 2020: nflscrapR and nflfastR start years. [05:08]
- "No NFL teams went for fourth down more than 50% of the time when the model said they should" over a 5-year span, versus more than half of teams by 2021. [06:09]
- About three times the fourth-down attempts per team per game of the 1980s, almost twice those of the 2000s. [06:40]
- Coverage disguised on more than half of snaps, first seen in 2021 (Rams). [08:12]
- 2018 to 2021: period when interior defensive linemen were valued below edge players. [09:45]
- Tracking data: every tenth of a second. [11:16]
- Fourth and one and a half versus fourth and an inch: the example of why inputs matter for judging a decision. [11:47]
- Offensive line and receiver papers were from "2024 or 2023." [13:49]
- Last six slides in about five years versus the first six over 40 years. [16:20]
- 95%: how far to meet football staff. A rule of thumb, not a measurement. [18:23]
- 21 million versus 16 million: a hypothetical free agency valuation used to illustrate uncertainty. [23:00]
- Wins above replacement, expected points added, win probability: named, not defined in the talk. [09:14]
- Possible caption garbles: "Sebastian Carl" (nflfastR co-creator, caption spelling), "Audie Weiner" and "Ryan Brill" (caption spelling), "SumerSports," "Huddle," "Brandt Tilis," "Telemetry," and "scrape bar" and "fast star" in the Q&A (nflscrapR and nflfastR). [05:08] [13:18] [18:23] [25:02]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Expected points added and win probability from play-by-play data. [05:38]
- Wins above replacement (Yurko's paper for quarterbacks, receivers, running backs and tight ends; a PFF version using PFF grades). [09:14]
- Event data (one row per player per play) versus tracking data. [10:46] [11:16]
- Big Data Bowl 2020 neural network (called pre-transformer) versus current transformer credit attribution. [14:19]
- Offensive line pass protection set depth and its stability across weeks; receiver depth when the ball is in the air. [13:18]
- Speaking in probabilities and error bars so that successive valuations overlap. [23:30] [24:01]

## Limits and open questions

- This is a survey talk with no new model, sample sizes or validation shown; the captions do not include slide content.
- Most of the history is the speaker's own account, and he has worked at PFF and the Panthers; the talk is presented by Sigma Computing.
- The AFC Championship game example is referred to but the detail is off the page in the captions. [16:51]
- The claim that recent progress exceeds the prior 40 years is given as his impression, not a measure. [16:20]
- Claims that AI tools will keep accelerating work are his expectation, not a result.
- He says the Dickerson trade was "the year prior" and then "2 years prior" (a self-correction in the captions). [03:35]

## Q&A

- Will pose data come to the NFL, how soon, and what would it answer that X and Y cannot? He expects it within the next few years and names technique and injury risk. [20:26] [20:57] [21:27]
- How do you explain changing results to staff without dumbing things down? Speak in probabilities and error bars so the distributions overlap. [22:28] [23:30] [24:01]
- How was older data cleaned for this growth? Data engineering and curation are unglamorous and still where teams and companies fall short. [24:32] [25:02] [26:05]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: JHgeEo3n1do
title: "SSAC26: Tackling Causality: Estimating Frame Level Defensive Impact"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Jenkins]
topics: [american-football, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Jenkins, a PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, presents a causal model for crediting defenders in American football. Traditional metrics credit only the tackler, and predictive models favor high-volume tacklers. His framework models all 22 players jointly with a transformer, estimates expected points saved for each defender by comparing expected points added with and without that defender's tackle, and uses propensity weighting and doubly robust estimation. On the first 9 weeks of a 2022 season it credits set-up defenders, ranks known top players better than supervised models, and aggregates to team results. He calls it a proof of concept.

## Key claims

- Football has a defensive attribution problem: on a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler though several defenders contributed. [00:00] [00:31]
- Supervised models predict outcomes, mix correlation with causation, favor high-volume tacklers and struggle to separate skill from opportunity. [01:01] [01:31]
- Causal inference asks what would have happened without the defender; it isolates individual contributions and separates player from scheme better, but needs more assumptions and quality control and cannot be applied in every scenario. [01:31] [02:01]
- Defenders do not act independently, so the model covers coordination, interference (for example, a defensive end setting the edge so a linebacker can tackle) and substitution effects, which violate independence. [02:31] [03:01] [03:31]
- The framework, called expected points saved, treats a defender making the tackle as the treatment and expected points added as the outcome. [04:02] [04:33]
- It uses a transformer over all 22 players, a propensity score model, an outcome model and inverse propensity weighting. [04:33] [05:04] [05:35]
- On the example play, the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive credit, which the speaker says shows the model captures coordinated effort. [06:09]
- Aaron Donald's expected points saved is around 0.27. [06:40]
- The method ranks players who earned All-Pro or Pro Bowl honors better than supervised models. [07:09] [07:39]
- Mean individual values aggregate to team level and explain 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes. [07:39]
- On synthetic data the method shows higher R-squared and lower RMSE than independent models, and ranks non-rookie players better against salaries and Pro Bowl status. [08:40]
- 68% of plays show significant interference effects, and modeling them reduces bias. [08:40] [09:10]
- The speaker calls it the first multi-agent causal inference framework in professional football for defensive evaluation; it is a proof of concept using the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season. [09:10]
- Intended next steps are quarterback decision-making and defensive back evaluation; stated uses are player evaluation, contract decisions and defensive scheme optimization. [09:41] [10:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Expected points saved: expected points added on the play when the defender does not make the tackle, minus expected points added when he does (as described). [04:02]
- Expected points added: the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits on a play. [04:02]
- Treatment: a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle. [04:02]
- 6-yard loss: the example running play. [00:00]
- 0.27: Aaron Donald's expected points saved; the speaker says each of his tackles prevents about 0.27 expected points. The captions describe the orange and blue distributions inconsistently (which is tackle and which is no tackle). [06:40] [07:09]
- 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes explained at team level. [07:39] [08:10]
- 68% of plays with significant interference effects. [08:40] [09:41]
- 9 weeks: the data available ("first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season"). [09:10]
- Data source named: 2024 NFL Big Data Bowl tracking data. [00:31]
- R-squared, RMSE, rank correlations and salary comparisons: stated as better, with no values in the captions. [08:40]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Interference-aware causal framework with a multi-agent transformer over 22 players. [02:31] [04:33]
- A directed acyclic graph with features: each defender's position, speed and direction, ball carrier features, relational features, 10 teammates, opponents and game context. [04:33] [05:04]
- Propensity score model and outcome model, with inverse propensity weighting to make a pseudo-population; doubly robust estimation for protection against model misspecification. [05:04] [05:35] [09:41]
- Validation by synthetic data, team-level aggregation, Pro Bowl and All-Pro agreement and salary rank. [07:39] [08:40]

## Limits and open questions

- Proof of concept on 9 weeks of one season, as the speaker says. [09:10]
- The talk does not say how many plays per defender, how the propensity model is checked, or how the treatment is defined for players who do not tackle but get credit.
- The video description mentions adversarial representation balancing, Bayesian uncertainty, and sensitivity analyses; none is described in the captions.
- Validation uses synthetic data and honors; real causal effects are not observable, as the speaker notes. [08:10]
- Scheme and assignment are not in the data; a questioner raised blitzers versus droppers, and the speaker's partial answer is propensity weighting, with scheme data expected to improve estimates. [11:43] [12:43]
- Claims of being first and of better ranking are the author's own and come from a competition presentation.
- "Tackle" here is the treatment; the audience question about pass rush disruption is answered only in general terms. [11:13]

## Q&A

- Does it handle pass plays and disruption without a tackle, such as Aaron Donald in the backfield? Yes, he gets positive credit for forcing the ball carrier elsewhere or lowering the odds a pass is beneficial. [10:43] [11:13]
- How does scheme (a blitzing linebacker versus a dropping one) confound the metric, and how would a team use scheme data? Ongoing research on scheme and responsibility; propensity weighting up-weights a low-probability defender's tackle; scheme data would improve estimates. [11:43] [12:17] [12:43]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: JjeFktc4QLM
title: "SSAC26: Deep Reinforcement Learning for NBA Player Valuation"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Jenkins]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Jenkins presents a deep reinforcement learning model that learns NBA player value from game outcomes, treating basketball as a sequence of states, actions and rewards, and splits team value among players with a neural approximation of Shapley values. He argues that identical box score actions have very different win impact depending on game state, that defense and off-ball value are missed by box score metrics, and that player synergy is measurable and predictive. He reports faster stabilization than regularized adjusted plus-minus, a Rudy Gobert example, 89 positive and 61 negative synergies, and better game prediction than traditional metrics, though the Vegas line remains best.

## Key claims

- Winning depends on context: the same made three-pointer matters more late in a close game, and value depends on teammates, opponents and interactions among the five on the floor. [00:00] [00:31]
- PER, win shares and box plus-minus aggregate box score statistics with fixed weights, overweight scoring, struggle with defense and lack context. [01:01] [01:31]
- Adjusted and regularized adjusted plus-minus regress possession outcomes on players on the floor but assume context-invariant contributions and miss synergy. [01:31]
- Sequential models such as expected possession value capture context and flow but struggle to credit individual players; the talk proposes deep reinforcement learning to combine both. [02:02] [02:32]
- In the example, a made three in the first quarter with a 15-point lead changed win probability by 2%, while one in the fourth quarter of a tied game with 1:30 left changed it by 23%; the speaker calls this a 10 times difference. [03:04]
- The model treats basketball as a Markov decision process and uses an advantage function for context-aware value. [04:05] [04:35]
- It values on-ball actions by action type, role and context, and values defense and off-ball influence by presence and constraints, not individual actions. [04:35] [05:07]
- Shapley values allocate team value by replacing each player with a learned baseline embedding; a neural approximation is used for computation. [05:38] [06:08]
- Compared with regularized adjusted plus-minus, the method needs about 67% fewer possessions for comparable accuracy and stabilizes in about 3 weeks versus 2 months. [06:38] [07:08]
- Action values peak in close clutch games, where a three-pointer can be worth more than double the traditional value, and diminish in blowouts; offensive rebounds and steals are valued significantly. [07:39]
- Jokic ranks first in the top 15; the ranking agrees substantially with regularized adjusted plus-minus and worse with box plus-minus, which the speaker ties to defensive valuation. [08:09] [08:40]
- Rudy Gobert ranks 54th on traditional metrics and 12th on this method; the box score missed 45% of his defensive value. [09:10]
- Defensive specialists are systematically undervalued by traditional metrics, a potential competitive advantage, and complementary skills matter in roster construction. [09:40]
- The study found 89 positive and 61 negative synergies, and traditional metrics wrongly assume player values add. [10:10] [10:41]
- Two equally talented rosters can differ by five or more wins because of fit, and adding synergy explains some unexplained variance. [11:11] [11:42]
- Adding the model to a Vegas line benchmark improves prediction, and adding synergy improves it further, though the Vegas line alone is best. [11:42] [12:12]
- In a capped league, winning comes from optimizing interactions, not collecting stars. [12:43]

## Numbers and definitions

- 2% versus 23%: win probability change for a low-leverage and a high-leverage made three. The speaker calls it a 10 times difference (23 divided by 2 is about 11.5, so "10 times" is approximate as spoken). [03:04]
- 67% fewer possessions than regularized adjusted plus-minus for comparable accuracy. [06:38]
- 3 weeks versus 2 months to stabilize. [07:08]
- Clutch three-pointer value can exceed traditional value by "more than double." [07:39]
- Gobert: 54th traditional, 12th by the model; 45% of defensive value missed. [09:10]
- 89 positive synergies and 61 anti-synergies. [10:10]
- Five or more wins: fit difference between equally talented rosters. [11:11]
- About five seasons of play-by-play data, "thousands of games." [16:21]
- Win residual: the difference between actual results and the model's prediction. [11:11]
- Advantage function: expected value of an action beyond the baseline state expectation. [04:35]
- Predictive accuracy figures: shown only on a chart, not stated in the captions. [11:42]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Markov decision process with states, actions, stochastic transitions and rewards in expected points and win probability. [04:05] [04:35]
- Temporal-difference learning and a distributional win-probability model appear in the video description but are not described in the captions.
- Neural Shapley value approximation with baseline player embeddings. [06:08]
- A comparison of synergy: on-court versus off-court pair performance, shown in a two-way quadrant plot. [10:10]
- Player dropout as a technique to swap each player for a neutral embedding and measure the change in win prediction. [14:16] [14:46]
- Benchmarks: regularized adjusted plus-minus, box plus-minus, and a Vegas line. [08:09] [11:42]
- "DRPM" appears once in the captions for the model's name (caption spelling). [15:49]

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker shows no player-level confidence intervals or exact accuracy numbers in the captions.
- A judge noted that Shapley values are contextual and not designed to be portable across lineups, yet validation sums them to predict games. The speaker agreed and pointed to synergy and player dropout as partial fixes. [13:13] [14:16]
- Sample size is a problem for new players and pairs who nearly always play together (Jokic and Murray, as captioned). [16:21]
- Predictive validation falls short of the Vegas line. [11:42]
- The defensive value claims (Gobert) rest on the model, with no independent check named.
- The claim that two equal rosters differ by five or more wins is reported without how it was computed. [11:11]
- The 67% and "3 weeks versus 2 months" figures are stated separately and not reconciled.
- Claims of market inefficiency are the author's view. [09:40]

## Q&A

- Validation sums Shapley contributions although they are contextual; how to improve? Player dropout with a neutral embedding, summed over the five on the court, is expected to do better. [13:13] [14:16] [14:46]
- How does Shapley handle two players who nearly always play together? The model accounts for who is on the court, and five seasons of play-by-play data limit the sample problem, though new players need extrapolation. [15:19] [15:49] [16:21]

title: "SSAC26: From Noise to Knowledge: Building High Quality Data Driven Research for Female Athletes"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: ["Kate Ari (caption spelling), director, co-founder and president of the Women's Health and Sports Performance Institute"]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, policy, decision-making]

## Summary

The speaker, a sports medicine physician and endocrinologist who co-founded a women's health and sports performance institute, argues that research on female athletes is thin and often poorly built. She gives the history of excluding women from research, the health burdens female athletes face, and the results of literature audits that score studies on population, athlete caliber, menstrual status method, journal and sample size. She warns about unvalidated wearables, weak hormone measurement, survey bias and AI repeating errors, and offers a workflow for validating wearable data. Her answer to closing the gap is teamwork across clinicians, athletes and data analysts.

## Key claims

- Women's sport is growing: Title IX, women now have 44% of sport opportunities, more than 160 female sports leagues exist, and fandom has risen, but gaps remain in media investment and prize money. [03:06] [03:35] [04:07] [06:40]
- Female athletes face higher rates of concussion, ACL tears and bone stress injuries, and relative energy deficiency in sport is very prevalent, partly through inadvertent under-fueling. [06:40] [07:10]
- Team USA athletes asked for research on pregnancy and postpartum, menstrual cycle symptoms, birth control, fueling across the cycle, mental health, recovery and more female coaches. [07:42] [08:12] [08:43]
- It is not known when sex differences change training, because they are not studied enough or studied well. [08:43] [09:14]
- Women of childbearing potential were excluded from early drug trials from 1977 until the early 1990s; drugs in common use have different pharmacokinetics and adverse reactions in women. [09:14] [10:16] [10:46]
- Women's health gets a small share of private health investment despite an estimated return on investment, and research funding does not match burden of disease (obstetric complications affect 33% of birthing women worldwide, yet only 2% of US registered trials address obstetrics). [11:48] [12:20] [12:51]
- Sports medicine textbooks historically treated female athletes as a "special population," and the speaker refused to write such a chapter, asking instead for each chapter to say what is known and unknown in women. [13:21] [13:51]
- Only 6% of articles in top sports medicine and science journals from 2014 to 2020 focused solely on women. [14:21]
- Her group audits the literature on population, athlete caliber (tiers 0 to 5), menstrual status method, research theme, journal impact and sample size. [14:53] [15:23] [15:54] [16:25] [16:56]
- Asking about menstrual status is not the same as testing hormones, and a withdrawal bleed on a birth control pill is not a natural cycle. [16:25]
